column4: The magicians state the section's sentence exactly: the criminal has Hell, where he neither dies nor lives; their warning turns Pharaoh's threat into the choice's final horizon.
Death comes to the tyrant from every direction yet he is not dead, making concrete the section's state in which torment removes life's good without completing death.
The Fire's people are neither finished by a decree of death nor relieved of punishment, the same suspended condition developed from 87:13.
The people of the Fire ask Mālik to have their Lord finish them, but are told they will remain, directly joining desired death to the section's terrible kind of staying.
The worldly life is diversion and play while the Hereafter is al-ḥayawān, the true life; this is the section's lexical claim that real life belongs to what lasts.
At judgment the person wishes he had sent something ahead “for my life,” locating his real life after the nearer life, just as the section does.
The transgressor “preferred the worldly life,” virtually repeating 87:16 and identifying the choice that produces the section's nonlife.
This ayah gives Hell as the refuge of the person in 79:38, completing the same preference-to-Fire movement that the section draws from 87:16 back to 87:13.
Pharaoh claims that his punishment is harsher and more lasting, appropriating أَبْقَىٰ for a mortal threat that the magicians answer with God's permanence.
The magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh and limit his power to “this worldly life,” exposing the boundary of the punishment he had called lasting in 20:71.
The magicians declare God “better and more lasting,” answering Pharaoh's أَبْقَىٰ and anticipating the exact pairing of 87:17.
Coming to God as a believer with righteous deeds yields the highest ranks, supplying the living positive destination opposite the criminal's nonlife in 20:74.
Eternal gardens are the reward of the one who purifies himself; this places the purification of 87:14 directly beside the lasting-life contrast of 20:74.
Flood foam disappears while what benefits people remains on earth; benefit and remaining meet here exactly as the section's definitions of life and lastingness require.
Satan offers Adam “the tree of immortality” and a kingdom that does not decay, the section's counterfeit promise of lasting life.
Abraham assigns both his death and subsequent revival to his Lord, placing the two endpoints denied in Hell under divine agency.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, a direct formulation of the section's passing-near versus lasting choice.
Worldly wealth and children are adornment, but “the lasting righteous deeds” are better in reward and hope, joining the section's خَيْرٌ and أَبْقَىٰ logic.
“The lasting righteous deeds” are better in reward and return, repeating the section's union of goodness and permanence.
The flower of worldly life is a test, whereas the Lord's provision is “better and more lasting,” almost restating 87:16-17.
Whatever people receive is worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is “better and more lasting,” the section's two lives stated as alternatives.
Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is “better and more lasting” for believers, exactly articulating the section's valuation.
Everyone upon the earth is passing away, naming the vanishing side of the section's contrast with what remains.
The Lord's majestic face remains after all on earth passes in 55:26, giving permanence its absolute referent.
Everything is perishing except God's face, a comprehensive boundary between created continuance and the permanence the section values.
“The remainder from God is better” joins بَقِيَّة and خَيْرٌ in one phrase, closely matching the section's claim that good is what truly remains.
Those who buy worldly life at the price of the Hereafter receive punishment that is not lightened, joining the wrong exchange to unrelieved torment.
The question “Are you content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter?” names the same preference and declares worldly enjoyment slight by comparison.
Those content and at ease with worldly life do not expect the meeting with God, specifying the stance behind the section's preference.
Fire is the refuge earned by the worldly contentment described in 10:7, completing the same choice and destination as 87:16 and 87:13.
Those who desire worldly life and its adornment may receive their works in it, isolating the near reward they chose.
For the people of 11:15, nothing awaits in the Hereafter but Fire and their works collapse, showing the near life's apparent benefit ending in the section's nonlife.
Those who love worldly life over the Hereafter enact the same preference as 87:16 and bend others away from God's path.
Loving worldly life more than the Hereafter is given as the reason for rejection, an explicit parallel to the section's diagnosis of preference.
Whoever wants the immediate life may receive some of it, then is assigned Hell; “the immediate” restates the nearness contained in الدُّنْيَا.
Whoever wants the Hereafter and strives for it in faith has an appreciated effort, the positive choice set against 17:18's immediate life and Hell.
The believing man calls worldly life only an enjoyment and the Hereafter the home of settled permanence, directly restating the section's temporal contrast.
The claim that there is only worldly life, in which “we die and live” and time destroys, is the false worldview that cannot see the section's real, later life.
Worldly life is likened to rain-grown vegetation that withers into debris before the lasting outcomes of the Hereafter, joining the surah's passing growth to this section's choice.
“You love the immediate” expresses worldly preference through nearness rather than the noun الدُّنْيَا.
“And leave the Hereafter” completes 75:20's choice in the same two-part form as 87:16-17.
People love the immediate life and leave behind a weighty day, restating the section's near-life preference and its hidden consequence.
Every soul tastes death, full recompense comes later, and worldly life is deceptive enjoyment; ordinary death and the near life's false value are held together.
A thousand years of life would not move the covetous person away from punishment, proving that mere duration is not the beneficial, lasting life of the section.
God takes souls at death and during sleep, retaining those decreed to die and returning the others; this directly realizes the source section's secondary death-as-sleep sense.
Human beings were dead, were given life, will die, and will be revived, laying out the divinely ordered endpoints from which the Fire's inmate is suspended.
The condemned confess two deaths and two givings of life, recognizing the full sequence whose final punishment cannot be escaped by another death.
Moses falls stricken and then, when he recovers, speaks; the sequence matches the source dictionary's “moutah” as a collapse from which one later regains consciousness.
Believers are told to answer God and the Messenger when called to what gives them life, exemplifying the section's definition of life as benefit and good.
Faithful good action is answered with “a good life,” explicitly uniting life with goodness against the useless continuance described in the Fire.
Every living thing is made from water, a Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's life-giving water called al-ḥayawān.
Pharaoh's people slaughter sons and يَسْتَحْيُونَ women, using life language in the source section's precise sense of sparing and keeping alive.
Pharaoh vows to kill the Israelites' sons and يَسْتَحْيِي their women, again making “give life” mean leave alive under selective extermination.
The recalled oppression pairs slaughtering sons with يَسْتَحْيُونَ women, exactly illustrating the dictionary sense of preserving someone alive.
Moses recalls Pharaoh's slaughter of sons and يَسْتَحْيُونَ women, the same survival sense of the life root cited by the section.
Pharaoh slaughters sons and يَسْتَحْيِي women, showing life as being spared from eradication rather than as flourishing.
The command to kill believers' sons and يَسْتَحْيُوا their women repeats the section's “keep alive” sense within a renewed threat of extermination.
“Do you see any remnant of them?” uses بَاقِيَة after annihilation, matching the source dictionary's contrast between being spared and being eradicated.
God destroyed Thamūd and “spared none,” using أَبْقَىٰ for the exact opposite of the source dictionary's plea to be left alive.
Noah's descendants are made “the survivors,” a direct Quranic instance of ب ق ي as preservation through threatened extinction.
Worldly life is rain-fed vegetation that becomes dry matter scattered by wind, supplying the vanishing side for the lasting deeds of 18:46.
Worldly life is rain, mingled growth, sudden ruin, and a field as if it had not flourished yesterday; the scene makes the near life's passing character visible.
Burned skins are repeatedly replaced so punishment can continue to be tasted, a concrete mechanism for torment that neither benefits as life nor concludes in death.
The Fire's people want to leave but cannot and have lasting punishment, joining denied escape to the section's destructive permanence.
Each attempt to leave the Fire from anguish returns its people to it, showing continued existence without the release of death.
Whenever the defiantly wicked seek to leave the Fire they are returned to it, another concrete form of the section's inescapable nonlife.
Faced with judgment, the condemned person wishes the first death had been final, voicing the desire for completion that the Fire refuses.
Cast into a constricted place in the Fire, its people call for destruction, seeking an end rather than the suspended continuance described by the section.
They are told to call not for one destruction but many, intensifying the impossible wish for extinction begun in 25:13.
The ayah moves through human life, death, powerless old age, and rain that makes lifeless earth stir and grow, gathering several of the section's distinctions between force, life, and revival.
Purifying rain gives life to a dead land and drink to creatures, directly paralleling the source dictionary's water that imparts life.
God's mercy revives the earth after its death, and the ayah explicitly carries that act over to reviving the dead.
Winds raise clouds, rain revives dead land, and the ayah identifies this as the pattern of resurrection.
Dead earth is revived and made to yield grain people eat, coupling restored life with concrete benefit.
Rain makes humbled earth stir and swell, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead.
Measured water revives a dead land and becomes the stated likeness for human emergence from death.
Rain-fed provision gives life to a dead land and is made the image of emergence, uniting life, benefit, and resurrection.
Water from heaven revives earth after death, a direct recurring form of water as the bearer of life.
Rain revives earth after its death, again placing life-giving water against lifelessness.
Heavenly water revives earth after death within a catalogue of signs, repeating the section's water-life association.
Provision descending from heaven revives earth after death, presenting life as bestowed nourishment and renewal.
Water revives earth after its death and disperses living creatures, bringing the life root, water, and benefit into one sign.
Heavy clouds deliver water and fruit from dead country, then the scene is explicitly compared with bringing out the dead.
God revives earth after its death, an explicit sign that life can be restored after apparent power has gone.
God is “the Living who does not die”; His deathlessness is perfect life, sharply distinguishing it from the Fire's inmate who does not die yet also does not live.
The people of the Garden taste no death beyond the first death, making deathlessness the condition of true reward rather than the Fire's suspended nonlife.
The Garden's speaker asks whether they will die no more, setting up joyous permanence as the reverse of Hell's inability to die.
“Except our first death, and we will not be punished” joins no further death to freedom from torment, precisely distinguishing paradise's deathlessness from 87:13.
Those killed in God's way must not be called dead but alive, distinguishing hidden, beneficial life from biological appearance.
The slain are alive with their Lord and provided for, coupling true life with benefit and provision rather than mere continuance.
One who was dead is made alive and given light, opposite one trapped in darkness unable to emerge; this moral life has the usefulness missing from the section's Fire.
The living and the dead are not equal, and responsiveness to hearing marks the difference; this supplies a moral sense of life beyond bodily duration.
The warning addresses whoever is alive while judgment becomes due against rejecters, using life for receptive capacity and making its benefit explicit.
The successful person is in “a pleasing life,” a positive realization of the source definition that life entails benefit and good.
The one whose scales are heavy is likewise in “a pleasing life,” the repeated positive counterpart to continued existence without good.
No human before the Prophet was granted immortality; earthly death is universal, so indefinite continuation cannot make the nearer life permanent.
The fruit of the two lasting gardens is دَانٍ, near at hand, showing that nearness itself can belong to the Hereafter and need not mean the transient الدُّنْيَا.
Paradise has clusters دَانِيَة, brought near, relocating the section's nearness root inside the true lasting life.
Garden shade is دَانِيَة over its people and fruit is lowered within reach, a concrete afterlife reversal of nearness as the worldly life's label.
The Helpers يُؤْثِرُونَ others over themselves, using the section's preference verb for a saving, generous choice rather than preference for the nearer life.
The criminals abide in Hell's punishment, establishing the enduring scene whose desperate request receives the answer “you will remain” in 43:77.
Punishment is not slackened and its people despair, specifying the absence of life's relief within the abiding scene of 43:74-77.
The Fire's people ask its keepers for even one day of reduced punishment, showing how continued time there lacks benefit or respite.
The cave sleepers look awake though they are asleep and are physically turned, staging sleep as a deathlike state without completed death.
The sleepers are “raised,” then ask how long they remained, joining recovery from deathlike sleep to the section's language of staying.
God takes people by night and raises them by day until their appointed term, a direct Quranic pattern behind the source's sleep-as-death sense.
Sleep is made repose and daytime “resurrection,” presenting waking as return from a deathlike interval.
Those raised from graves call them their sleeping place, bringing sleep, death, and awakening into the same scene.
After the thunderbolt death, the Israelites are raised again, matching the section's collapse-and-recovery edge of the death root.
One trumpet blast fells creation and the next makes them stand, placing collapse and recovery at the cosmic threshold of death and life.
God creates from weakness, gives strength, then makes weakness follow strength; this bodily arc concretely displays the withdrawal of force used to define death in the section.
Some are returned to the feeblest age and lose former knowledge, an earthly case in which life's biological continuation no longer guarantees retained power or benefit.
Whomever God grants long life is reversed in creation, qualifying the assumption that more duration by itself is better life.
The hoarder imagines his wealth has made him immortal, another false worldly permanence parallel to Satan's offer of the tree of immortality.
The people build monumental structures as though they might live forever, exposing worldly works aimed at counterfeit permanence.
Noah and his family are rescued from great distress, supplying the act of preservation whose surviving descendants are named in 37:77.
After Noah and those with him are saved, “the remaining ones” are drowned, using ب ق ي for those left behind who are then eradicated.
Saqar “neither spares nor leaves,” a severe use of the section's ب ق ي sense: the fire consumes without granting its victim the completion of death.
Later heirs seize the goods of “this nearer/lower” life while presuming forgiveness, using أَدْنَى for the morally chosen immediate gain.
الدُّنْيَا names the nearer side of the valley, preserving the literal spatial nearness from which the source section says worldly life receives its name.
The harvest metaphor divides desire for the Hereafter from desire for the worldly crop, and the latter yields no share in the Hereafter.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the Hereafter's home is better for the mindful, a concise valuation parallel to 87:16-17.
Desirable worldly things are beautified as the enjoyment of this life, while the good return is with God, setting up the “better than this” offer in 3:15.
Gardens and lasting divine approval are announced as better than the worldly attractions of 3:14, spelling out the section's better alternative.
Rain-grown crops flourish, yellow, and become debris as a reminder, a concrete passing-life scene that supports the section's distinction between what fades and remains.
The magicians fall in prostration and affirm the Lord of Aaron and Moses; this act identifies the speakers whose worldly-life refusal leads to 20:74-76.
The wind and purifying water introduce the life-giving act of 25:49, contributing the water itself rather than the following ayah's revival.
Blessed water descends and grows gardens and grain, beginning the provision-and-revival sequence completed in 50:11.
Tall palms with clustered fruit add the nourishment that makes the water's restored life beneficial before 50:11 names dead-land revival.
The verb دَنَا means “came near,” and may illuminate the source's derivation of الدُّنْيَا from nearness, though its revelatory scene does not itself concern worldly life's transience.
The hypocrites would follow for a near gain and easy journey; this is a specific instance of visible nearness winning preference, though it does not explicitly contrast the two lives.
